Military Advanced Pati Diver here. Not Cave certified. The distance is a real bitch, but the should be able to run a line, like they do with hard hat diving. The obvious concern is that the longer the hose, the more resistance, although we can pump air hundreds of feet deep, which add a lot more resistance than the hose itself. Every 33 feet is 1 atmosphere. If you took a full lung breath at sea level, and descended to 33 feet, you would literally have half the volume of air in your lungs. 66 feet 1/3... so on. So you can imagine how hard you have to work to compress air to depth. This doesn't appear to be the case in this cave according to what I've seen, so the primary resistance is to running such a long distance.

You also have to factor pressure. You cant just pump air into an enclosed space. With any gas, Pressure and temperature have an inverse relationship to volume. So if you pump air with no increase in volume, the temperature and pressure will increase. Temperature is not a problem, but PSI has a way of moving shit you wouldn't expect to move. That means as you pump air in, you have to pump air out equally. This is very difficult when your compressor is a mile away.

The diver died while transporting tanks. If he himself was using traditional scuba jugs, he was probably tangled up (fouled) in the narrow part. Possibly he lost his regulator to a foul and didn't have the ability to reattach. If there wasn't so much air required, you would NEVER try and make it through a narrow passage with twin 80s or whatever he had, especially while towing a load. You would either run a line from a set of tanks set before the water begins, or you would use a rebreather, which filters your exhaust and injects a small amount of O2 into the stream. Even while carrying a load, I have no idea why he didn't use a rebreather, even if only for the narrow portion, ideally with a set of tanks set aside with only O2 to refill his rebreather, and a line run from the surface from a set of tanks on the surface in the cave as a backup.

Now, everyone thinks Scuba is easy. They are right... until something goes wrong. How do you train for that? First, you force people to screw up badly to the point where they take a big breath of water. The group will drop by about 90%. The remaining 10% are the ones that have the quirk that allows them to experience drowning and stay calm. Lifelong varsity swimmers in my class were the first ones to drop. They are very good at not drowning, and haven't really taken a panic gulp in years. After that, we had Hits. Search 'NDSTC Hits'. It's the instructors simulating you getting fouled. Some are about untangling, but we always remember the instructors that simulated violent fouls, where the 'environment' decides it is going to smash the top of your jugs into your head and scrape your face on the bottom of the pool. A Sea-bee chief Perrault was a legend at this. Point is, these kids are going to try and go through and they are going to get fouled, they will be weak from being stuck in a cave, and they will panic. You can't just slap a tank on them and shove them through. If they panic, the Seals will die trying to save them.

It might even be easier to knock them unconscious, slap a mask on their face, and pass them through like underwater luggage. Anyone who has spent some time here has seen how save it is to be around a swimming Nigerian. The reach and grab and snatch and pull until anyone within arms length is dead next to them.
